Once in a while, you meet someone who changes your idea of a place.
She said: Come back on Saturday, and I will introduce you.
What I remember most is how he smiled at the end.
She explained the custom clearly.
He spoke very quietly and smiled warmly.
The waiter reacted quite unexpectedly.
You speak English really well.
Good morning! You are looking at the sardines very carefully. Are you a chef?
No, just a curious tourist. Can I choose the fish myself?
You point, and I choose. That is the custom in this market. Locals never touch the fish.
Oh, I am sorry! I did not know. I hope it was only a small misunderstanding.
It is fine. You asked politely. Most tourists just grab a fish and pay quickly.
And how do you cook sardines at home?
Very simply: salt, olive oil and a hot grill. My grandmother used to say: Fish swims three times, in the sea, in the oil and in the wine.
That is a wonderful way to say it.
Come back on Saturday at seven. My brother brings the best fish, and I can introduce you. That is our hospitality.
She explained the custom very clearly.
Sorry, I think there was a small misunderstanding.
Thank you so much for your hospitality.
People here are a little reserved at first.

Once in a while, you meet someone who changes your idea of a whole country. In Ljubljana I went to the same small coffee shop every morning for a week. The owner was very reserved. On the first day he served me silently, and he didn't look at me once. On the second day he nodded slowly when I came in. On the third day he asked me, in careful English, where I was from. And on the last day he came to my table, put down a piece of cake that his wife made, and said: For the road. That week I learned something important. People in some places are not cold. They are just slow to open the door. If you come back patiently, the door opens.

My first big misunderstanding in Bulgaria was about my head. At a market in Sofia, I asked a woman if the tomatoes were fresh. She shook her head, so I said sorry and walked away. She called me back, very surprised, and almost angry. In Bulgaria, a shake of the head can mean yes, and a nod can mean no. Since that day I watch people carefully, and I listen to the words, not the head. Gestures are a language too, and nobody teaches it in a classroom. So my advice is simple. When a gesture confuses you, ask politely, with words. Locals are usually happy to explain, and the misunderstanding becomes a real conversation.

First he walked into the fish market in Split at eight in the morning and stopped at a small stall. Then he asked the woman if he could choose the fish himself, and she explained the custom very patiently. After that she told him how her grandmother used to cook sardines, simply, with salt and olive oil. At that point she wrote a note for him and invited him to come back on Saturday to meet her brother. In the end he thanked her warmly for her hospitality and walked away with the note in his pocket.
